case_analysis.focal_point: Whether venue for an 18 U.S.C. § 1519 obstruction-by-falsification prosecution is proper in the district where the targeted federal investigation is located, even if the defendant’s falsifying acts occurred entirely in another district.
case_analysis.legal_provision: 18 U.S.C. § 1519 (falsification of records in federal investigations) and the Constitution’s venue requirements (U.S. Const. art. III, § 2, cl. 3; Sixth Amendment Vicinage Clause).
case_analysis.petitioner_position: Petitioner argues venue is improper when no essential conduct element of the charged § 1519 offense occurred in the prosecuting district. In petitioner’s view, § 1519’s conduct element is the act of falsifying/altering/destroying a record, and its intent-to-obstruct language is only a mens rea element that cannot, by itself, supply venue based on contemplated or downstream effects in the district of the investigation. Allowing venue wherever the government investigation sits would untether venue from where the defendant acted, expand prosecutorial choice of forum, and conflict with constitutional venue protections that generally require trial where the crime’s conduct took place.
case_analysis.respondent_position: The United States argues venue is proper in the district of the investigation at which the falsification was directed. The government’s theory is that § 1519 defines an obstruction offense whose gravamen includes targeting (i.e., directing obstructive conduct at) a federal matter; therefore the locus delicti can include the district where the relevant investigation or matter is situated. On this view, trying the case where the obstructive impact is aimed—where investigators are located and where the proceeding/matter would be impeded—fits the statute’s purpose and standard venue principles for obstruction-type crimes.
key_precedents: Ciminelli v. United States, 598 U.S. 306 (2023) (rejection of the 'right-to-control' theory of wire fraud)
United States v. Percoco, 598 U.S. 319 (2023) (honest-services fraud limits; referenced in lower-court discussion)
United States v. Rodriguez-Moreno, 526 U.S. 275 (1999) (venue turns on essential conduct elements of the offense)
United States v. Cabrales, 524 U.S. 1 (1998) (venue improper where only effects/antecedent crimes occurred elsewhere)
United States v. Kellington, 217 F.3d 1084 (9th Cir. 2000) (new-trial standard; appears in the record excerpts)
United States v. Alston, 974 F.2d 1206 (9th Cir. 1992) (new-trial/weight-of-evidence standard; appears in record excerpts)

John Roberts.reasoning: I remain with petitioner because venue must follow the locus delicti by identifying the statute’s essential conduct elements and locating where that conduct occurred; §1519’s operative verbs describe a complete act of falsifying/altering/destroying/concealing records, all of which happened outside the charging district. The Government’s best contrary point—pressed in the conference as an investigation- or matter-centered theory of obstruction—treats the object of intent and anticipated effects as venue-conferring, but as Justice Kagan and Justice Kavanaugh underscore, Cabrales and Rodriguez-Moreno do not allow mens rea or downstream impact to substitute for conduct. Accepting that theory would untether venue from the defendant’s acts, invite forum shopping, and effectively convert §1519 into a roving, one-size-fits-all obstruction statute, potentially obviating more specific Chapter 73 provisions absent a clear congressional choice. Our holding can be narrow: where the charged §1519 conduct is completed entirely in one district and the statute contains no express venue rule keyed to an investigation’s situs, venue does not lie solely where the investigation is administered.

Clarence Thomas.reasoning: Respondent’s best contention is that §1519’s intent to impede a federal investigation makes the investigation’s situs part of the offense and thus a permissible venue anchor. But as the Chief Justice emphasizes, our locus-delicti inquiry turns on the statute’s essential conduct elements, and §1519’s conduct is limited to “falsifies, alters, destroys, mutilates, conceals, covers up, or makes a false entry” in a record; the investigation language supplies only the object of intent, not additional conduct occurring wherever agents happen to work. Justice Kagan’s point underscores the mismatch with Cabrales: we do not treat mens rea or anticipated downstream effects as venue-conferring acts absent a clear congressional directive. Congress has shown elsewhere that it can key venue to the location of a proceeding or investigation, and §1519 contains no such provision, so constitutional venue remains where the falsification occurred.

Samuel Alito.reasoning: The Government’s best argument—venue should lie where the federal investigation or “matter” is located because that is where the intended impairment is felt—cannot be reconciled with Article III’s venue language, which is keyed to where the “Crimes” were “committed,” i.e., where the defendant’s essential conduct occurred. As the Chief Justice and Justice Kavanaugh stress, our locus-delicti cases require identifying §1519’s conduct elements (falsifies/alters/destroys/conceals/makes a false entry) and locating them; the investigation language appears only in the intent clause and does not itself supply a place of commission. Treating an object-of-intent or downstream effects as venue-conferring would untether venue from conduct and invite the very forum-shopping the Constitution’s venue and vicinage provisions were designed to prevent, absent any clear textual venue rule from Congress. If venue was improper, the settled remedy is vacatur and retrial in the proper district; there is no historical or doctrinal basis to create an acquittal/dismissal-with-prejudice exception here.

Sonia Sotomayor.reasoning: The Government’s best argument remains that §1519 is aimed at interference with a federal “matter,” so venue should lie where that matter is administered or investigated. But as the Chief Justice and Justice Kagan emphasize, our locus-delicti cases require venue to track the statute’s essential conduct elements, and §1519’s heartland conduct is the falsification/alteration/destruction/concealment of records—completed where the defendant acted—not where investigators later sit. Reading the “matter” language (which appears in the intent clause) as venue-conferring would improperly convert mens rea and anticipated effects into conduct, contrary to Cabrales, and it would functionally create a roving venue rule Congress did not enact. Chapter 73’s structure reinforces the background rule: when Congress intends to dispense with ordinary limitations, it says so expressly, so we should not infer an effects-based venue exception from §1519’s intent language alone.

Elena Kagan.reasoning: The Government’s best venue theory—that §1519 is aimed at protecting a federal “matter” and so can be tried where that matter is investigated—still treats the object of intent as if it were a conduct element. As the Chief Justice and Justice Kavanaugh stress, our locus-delicti cases (Cabrales in particular) require separating actus reus from mens rea, and §1519’s operative conduct is confined to the falsification/alteration/destruction/concealment itself; the investigation/matter language sits in the intent clause and requires no obstructive act or effect in the forum. Accepting an investigation-situs venue rule would invite precisely the forum-shopping and dilution of vicinage protections Roberts warns about, and Congress’s silence here—when it knows how to write proceeding- or investigation-based venue rules—confirms we should apply the constitutional default. Venue therefore lies where the falsification occurred, not where federal agents later pursued the matter.

Neil Gorsuch.reasoning: The Government’s best point is that §1519 is aimed at protecting federal investigations, so venue should track the investigation’s situs. But as the Chief Justice stresses, our locus-delicti cases require us to identify the offense’s essential conduct elements and locate where that conduct occurred; here, the statute’s verbs—falsifies, alters, destroys, conceals, covers up, makes a false entry—supply the only conduct, while the investigation/matter language sits in the intent clause as an object-of-purpose and federal hook. Treating that mens rea object (or downstream effect on investigators) as venue-conferring would do what Cabrales warns against—turning purpose/effects into a roving venue rule—and, as Justice Kagan notes, invites forum shopping absent a clear congressional venue provision. On this record, with all falsification completed outside the charging district, constitutional venue must follow the defendant’s acts, not the government’s investigative geography.

Brett Kavanaugh.reasoning: I remain with petitioner. The Government’s strongest point—venue where the affected federal investigation or “matter” is located—treats the object of intent and downstream effects as if they were essential conduct, but under Cabrales and our locus-delicti framework venue must track the statute’s conduct elements. As Chief Justice Roberts and Justice Kagan stress, §1519’s operative verbs (falsifies, alters, destroys, conceals, makes a false entry) supply the only actus reus; the “intent to impede, obstruct, or influence” clause is mens rea and does not create a second locus where the offense is “committed.” Structurally, as Justice Thomas notes, Congress elsewhere writes express venue hooks keyed to proceedings when it wants them, and reading one into §1519 would invite forum shopping without clear textual authorization.

Amy Coney Barrett.reasoning: The Government’s strongest venue theory—that §1519 is aimed at a federal “matter” or “investigation” and so venue lies where that matter is administered—treats the object of intent as if it were an essential conduct element. As Chief Justice Roberts and Justice Kagan emphasize, the statute’s operative verbs supply the conduct (falsifies, alters, destroys, conceals, etc.), and the investigation/matter language appears only in the intent clause; under our locus-delicti cases, that does not relocate venue to wherever agents later investigate. Overlap with other obstruction statutes or breadth concerns does not justify atextually adding an effects-based venue rule; the limiting work is done by §1519’s intent requirement and the established obstruction nexus framework, not by untethering venue from the defendant’s acts.

Ketanji Brown Jackson.reasoning: The Government’s strongest point—that §1519 is an obstruction provision designed to protect federal investigations, so venue should lie where the investigation is centered—fails under our locus-delicti framework because it treats the object of intent (and anticipated effects) as if it were an essential conduct element. As Chief Justice Roberts and Justice Kagan underscore, the statute’s operative verbs define the prohibited conduct—falsifying/altering/destroying/concealing/making a false entry—and that conduct was completed in Seattle; the “intent to impede, obstruct, or influence” clause supplies mens rea and a federal hook, not additional conduct occurring wherever agents later investigate. Accepting an investigation-location theory would effectively add a broad venue provision Congress did not write, expanding forum choice in tension with Article III and the Sixth Amendment’s vicinage protections. The broader Chapter 73 context, as Justice Kavanaugh notes, confirms that when Congress wants venue keyed to a proceeding’s situs, it says so explicitly—so we should not infer that result from §1519’s intent language alone.

John Roberts.reasoning: Venue must be tied to the locus delicti of the charged offense, which we determine by identifying the statute’s essential conduct elements and locating where that conduct occurred. Section 1519’s operative conduct is the act of falsifying, altering, destroying, or concealing a record; the “intent to impede, obstruct, or influence” clause is a mens rea requirement that cannot, by itself, relocate venue to the district where an investigation happens to sit. Accepting the Government’s targeting/effects theory would untether venue from the defendant’s acts, invite forum shopping, and—without clear congressional direction—expand this evidence-focused provision into a broader, impact-based venue rule inconsistent with Article III and the Sixth Amendment’s vicinage protections. Because all falsifying acts occurred in another district, venue in the investigation’s district is improper.

Clarence Thomas.reasoning: The controlling question is the crime’s locus delicti, which turns on the “nature of the crime alleged and the location of the act or acts constituting it.” Section 1519’s only essential conduct is the falsifying/altering/destroying (or making a false entry in) a record; its “intent to impede, obstruct, or influence” language describes mens rea, not additional conduct occurring wherever an investigation happens to sit. Because the indictment and trial theory rest on falsification acts completed entirely in another district, venue cannot be anchored solely to the investigation’s location without converting a mental-state or downstream effect into a venue-conferring act—precisely what our venue cases forbid. The Constitution’s venue and vicinage protections require trial where the defendant’s criminal acts occurred, absent a statutory venue provision Congress actually enacted for § 1519.

Samuel Alito.reasoning: The Constitution’s venue provisions are keyed to where the alleged “Crimes” were “committed,” and our cases therefore ask for the locus delicti by identifying the offense’s essential conduct elements and the place where the acts constituting the offense occurred. On these facts, the only conduct criminalized by § 1519 is the act of falsifying/altering/destroying a record; the statute’s “intent to impede, obstruct, or influence” language is a mens rea element that cannot, standing alone, relocate venue to the district where the investigation sits when no part of the falsification occurred there. Treating the investigation’s location as sufficient would untether venue from the defendant’s acts and expand prosecutorial forum choice in a way that lacks firm textual or historical support. If venue was laid in the wrong district, the established remedy is vacatur and retrial in a proper venue, not dismissal with prejudice, and double jeopardy is not implicated.

Sonia Sotomayor.reasoning: Section 1519 contains no special venue clause, so under the constitutional venue commands and this Court’s locus-delicti cases we must identify the statute’s essential conduct and then locate where that conduct occurred. Read in statutory context, § 1519 is a specialized, later-enacted obstruction “extension” that criminalizes the act of falsifying/altering/destroying records with a federal-obstruction purpose; its heartland conduct is the falsification itself, while the reference to a federal “matter” or “investigation” functions as the object of intent (and jurisdictional hook), not an additional actus reus. Negative-implication logic from Chapter 73 reinforces that when Congress wants to anchor consequences to a particular forum (or to decouple requirements expressly), it says so; absent such direction, venue cannot rest solely on where investigators sit or where downstream effects may be felt. Because all falsifying acts occurred entirely outside the charging district, trying petitioner where the investigation was located would untether venue from the defendant’s conduct and conflict with the core constitutional protection that the trial occur where the crime was committed.

Elena Kagan.reasoning: Section 1519’s operative text makes the Government prove an actus reus—“falsif[ying],” “alter[ing],” “destroy[ing],” etc., a record—and then a mens rea—doing so “with the intent to impede, obstruct, or influence” a covered federal matter. Under Cabrales and Rodriguez-Moreno, venue tracks the “location of the act or acts constituting” the offense’s essential conduct, and here all falsifying acts occurred outside the prosecuting district; the investigation’s location describes only the object of the defendant’s intent, not conduct performed there. Accepting venue wherever the investigation sits would convert §1519 into an effects/target-based venue rule untethered from where the defendant acted, expanding prosecutorial forum choice in a way that conflicts with Article III and the Sixth Amendment’s vicinage protections. Nothing in §1519 supplies a contrary, congressionally specified venue rule, so the Constitution’s conduct-based default controls on these facts.

Neil Gorsuch.reasoning: Section 1519’s essential conduct is the falsifying/altering/destroying (or concealing) of a “record, document, or tangible object”; the statute’s reference to a federal “investigation or proper administration of any matter” goes to the object of the defendant’s intent, not an additional actus reus that occurs wherever investigators later sit. On these facts, all charged falsifying acts occurred entirely outside the prosecuting district, so anchoring venue to the investigation’s location would untether venue from where the defendant committed the proscribed conduct and expand prosecutorial forum choice in tension with Article III and the Sixth Amendment’s vicinage guarantee. Reading §1519 to allow venue wherever a contemplated investigation is located would also invite malleable, discretionary enforcement—turning a clear conduct-based statute into a free-floating venue lever keyed to downstream effects. Under the element-focused locus delicti inquiry, the only proper venue is where the defendant performed the falsification.

Brett Kavanaugh.reasoning: The Constitution’s venue provisions and our cases (especially Cabrales and Rodriguez-Moreno) require courts to identify the offense’s essential conduct elements and locate where that conduct occurred. Section 1519’s ordinary text makes the relevant conduct the act of falsifying/altering/destroying/concealing a record; the reference to an investigation or matter appears in the mens rea phrase (“with the intent to impede, obstruct, or influence”), and the statute does not require that any obstruction occur or that an investigation even be pending. Here, all falsifying acts occurred entirely in another district, and trying the case where investigators sit would improperly base venue on contemplated downstream effects or the object of the defendant’s intent rather than on conduct elements. Reading § 1519 in context with other obstruction statutes confirms Congress knows how to tie venue to a proceeding’s location when it wishes, and § 1519 does not do so.

Amy Coney Barrett.reasoning: The Constitution’s venue commands require tying trial location to the “locus delicti,” which we identify by looking to the offense’s essential conduct elements rather than its mens rea or downstream effects. Section 1519’s text makes the actus reus the falsifying/altering/destroying (or covering up) of a record; the “with the intent to impede, obstruct, or influence” language is a classic intent element that does not itself supply a place of commission, so venue cannot rest solely on where investigators sit. On these facts, all falsifying acts occurred entirely outside the prosecuting district, and anchoring venue in the investigation’s district would untether venue from the defendant’s conduct and expand forum choice in a way inconsistent with Article III and the Vicinage Clause. Any breadth concern is managed by §1519’s element requiring intent to obstruct a federal matter, but that targeting requirement does not convert the investigation’s location into an essential conduct location for venue purposes.

Ketanji Brown Jackson.reasoning: The Constitution fixes venue where the crime was “committed,” and our cases instruct that inquiry turns on the statute’s essential conduct elements, not on a defendant’s purpose or the hoped-for effects elsewhere. Section 1519’s text identifies the proscribed conduct as making/altering/falsifying (or destroying) a record; the remaining language describes the required intent with respect to a federal matter, but it does not add an element requiring any obstructive impact to occur in the investigation district. On these facts, the alleged falsification was created and completed in Seattle, so trying the case in the Northern District of California would improperly tether venue to the location of a federal investigation rather than to where the defendant’s conduct occurred—an expansion that risks converting § 1519 into a broad, effects-based venue provision without clear congressional command. Faithful, text-and-structure interpretation and rule-of-law restraint in criminal cases therefore require holding venue proper only in the district where the falsifying acts took place.

case_analysis.focal_point: Whether venue for a prosecution under 18 U.S.C. § 1519 is proper in the district where the federal investigation was located (and where the obstructive intent was directed), even if the defendant’s alleged falsification of records occurred entirely in a different district.
case_analysis.legal_provision: 18 U.S.C. § 1519 (falsification of records in federal investigations) and the constitutional/criminal-procedure venue requirements (Article III, Section 2, Clause 3; Sixth Amendment Vicinage Clause; Fed. R. Crim. P. 18).
case_analysis.petitioner_position: The petitioner argues venue must be tied to where the defendant committed the conduct element(s) of the offense (here, the alleged falsifying/altering/making of records), and cannot be established solely because the statute includes an intent element aimed at affecting an investigation in another district; allowing venue wherever an investigation sits improperly converts an effects- or intent-based theory into a venue rule, undermines the Constitution’s trial-in-the-state-and-district-of-the-crime guarantees, and invites government forum shopping by selecting a favorable investigation location rather than the locus of criminal acts.
case_analysis.respondent_position: The United States argues venue is proper in the district of the federal investigation that the falsification was intended to obstruct because § 1519 criminalizes obstructive falsification in relation to a federal matter, making the investigation district a legitimate locus of the offense’s completion or operative focus; when the obstructive conduct is directed at and designed to impair a specific federal investigation, trying the case where that investigation is based satisfies venue principles for crimes defined by their relationship to and interference with federal proceedings or matters.
key_precedents: Ciminelli v. United States, 143 S. Ct. 1121 (2023)
United States v. Kellington, 217 F.3d 1084 (9th Cir. 2000)
United States v. Alston, 974 F.2d 1206 (9th Cir. 1992)
United States v. Del Toro-Barboza, 673 F.3d 1136 (9th Cir. 2012)
United States v. Camacho, 555 F.3d 695 (8th Cir. 2009)

John Roberts.reasoning: The Government’s strongest point—pressed as Justice Kagan frames it—is an effects/aiming theory: § 1519 is an obstruction statute, so venue should lie where the contemplated federal matter or investigation is situated. But our locus-delicti cases direct us to the statute’s essential conduct elements, and § 1519’s operative verbs (falsifies, alters, destroys, conceals, covers up, makes a false entry) identify conduct completed where the records were manipulated, not where an investigation later proceeds. The “in relation to or contemplation of” phrase is best read as a circumstance/intent limiter that narrows federal reach; converting it into a roving venue hook would expand prosecutorial forum choice without a clear statement, undermining Article III and the Sixth Amendment vicinage guarantee, as Justices Thomas and Gorsuch caution. A narrow, administrable holding—venue lies where the falsification conduct occurred (or was begun/continued/completed), not merely where an investigation sits—preserves statutory coherence and constitutional baseline protections.

Clarence Thomas.reasoning: The strongest argument for Respondent would be that §1519’s “in relation to or contemplation of” language makes the federal matter’s situs—here, the investigation district—part of the offense such that venue may lie where the contemplated matter is located. But as Chief Justice Roberts and Justice Gorsuch emphasize, our venue cases look first to the statute’s essential conduct elements; §1519’s operative verbs (falsifies, conceals, covers up, makes a false entry) define the actus reus, and those acts occurred entirely elsewhere. The investigation’s location appears only as the object of intent/circumstance, and converting that into a venue hook would be an atextual effects-based theory that untethers venue from the defendant’s conduct and invites prosecutorial forum selection. Nothing in §1519 supplies a clear congressional directive to override the constitutional baseline tying trial to where the criminal conduct was committed.

Samuel Alito.reasoning: The Government’s best point—that §1519 is an obstruction statute and thus venue should lie where the contemplated federal matter or investigation is located—cannot be squared with our locus-delicti framework, which ties venue to essential conduct elements rather than to intent, anticipated effects, or the Government’s investigative choices. As Chief Justice Roberts explains, §1519’s operative verbs define the actus reus (falsifying/altering/destroying/concealing/making a false entry), and nothing in the text makes the situs of a federal investigation an element the Government must prove to obtain a conviction. Justice Thomas is right that converting the “in relation to or contemplation of” language into a roving venue hook would invite precisely the forum shopping the Venue and Vicinage Clauses were designed to prevent. If venue was improper, the appropriate remedy remains vacatur and retrial in a proper district, consistent with historical practice and our precedents, not an acquittal.

Sonia Sotomayor.reasoning: The Government’s strongest point is that § 1519 is designed to protect federal investigations, so venue should lie where the threatened federal matter sits. But as Chief Justice Roberts and Justice Kagan emphasize, our locus-delicti framework requires tying venue to the statute’s essential conduct elements, and § 1519’s operative verbs define conduct (falsifying/altering/destroying/concealing/making false entries) that occurred entirely in the other district. The “in relation to or contemplation of” language functions as a circumstance/intent limitation—much like the background obstruction “administration of justice” concept—rather than a clear congressional signal that Congress meant to displace the constitutional baseline and authorize effects-based, roving venue. Accepting the Government’s theory would turn mens rea and anticipated effects into a venue hook and invite forum selection by investigative siting, precisely what Article III and the Sixth Amendment are meant to constrain absent unmistakable statutory direction.

Elena Kagan.reasoning: The Government’s strongest point is that § 1519 is an obstruction statute and so venue should lie where the federal matter or investigation sits—an effects/aiming theory. But as Chief Justice Roberts and Justice Gorsuch stress, our locus-delicti precedents (Cabrales and Rodriguez-Moreno) tie venue to the statute’s essential conduct elements, and § 1519’s conduct verbs—“falsifies, alters, destroys … makes a false entry”—occurred only in Seattle here. The “in relation to or contemplation of” language does important limiting work by narrowing what the Government must prove about the defendant’s purpose and the federal nexus, but it does not supply a second actus reus in the investigation district; converting mens rea/circumstance into a roving venue hook would invite precisely the forum shopping the vicinage clauses are meant to prevent. Nothing in § 1519 gives the clear congressional instruction needed to depart from that constitutional baseline.

Neil Gorsuch.reasoning: The Government’s best point is that § 1519’s “in relation to or contemplation of” language makes the federal matter’s situs part of the offense and thus can anchor venue where that matter sits. But as the Chief Justice and Justice Kagan explain, our venue precedents ask where the statute’s essential conduct elements were committed; here, the verbs Congress chose—“falsifies, alters, destroys, conceals, covers up, [or] makes a false entry”—define the actus reus and occurred wholly in the other district. The investigation’s location is, at most, a circumstance or mens rea object that narrows the statute’s reach, and allowing it to supply venue would effectively convert intent/effects into a roving venue hook, inviting forum shopping without a clear congressional statement. Nothing in § 1519’s text speaks in venue terms or makes the investigation’s situs something the Government must plead and prove as an element of where the crime was committed.

Brett Kavanaugh.reasoning: The Government’s best point is purposive: § 1519 protects federal investigations, so venue should lie where the threatened investigation or matter is located. But as Chief Justice Roberts and Justice Kagan explain, our venue precedents (Cabrales/Rodriguez-Moreno) tie venue to the offense’s essential conduct elements, and § 1519’s operative conduct is “falsif[ying]” (or altering/destroying/concealing/making a false entry) a record—conduct completed in the other district on these facts. The “in relation to or contemplation of” clause functions as a mens rea/circumstance (and jurisdictional) limitation, not an additional actus reus occurring where investigators happen to sit, and treating it as a roving venue hook would invite prosecutorial forum selection without a clear congressional statement. A narrow holding, as the Chief suggests, preserves an administrable rule grounded in enacted text and the Article III/Sixth Amendment vicinage baseline.

Amy Coney Barrett.reasoning: The Government’s best point is an effects/aiming theory: because § 1519 protects federal investigations, venue should lie where the investigation is centered. But as Chief Justice Roberts and Justice Kagan emphasize, our locus-delicti framework keys venue to the statute’s essential conduct elements, and § 1519’s operative verbs—falsifies, alters, destroys, conceals, makes a false entry—were completed entirely in the other district on these facts. The investigation’s situs enters only through relational/intent language (“in relation to or contemplation of”), and treating that circumstance as a venue hook would let prosecutors manufacture venue by selecting an investigative location, undermining Article III and Sixth Amendment vicinage protections absent a clear congressional directive. A narrow rule suffices: when the charged § 1519 violation is fully consummated by document falsification in one district, venue cannot rest solely on where a contemplated federal matter or investigation happens to be located.

Ketanji Brown Jackson.reasoning: The Government’s strongest point is that § 1519’s “in relation to or contemplation of” language, coupled with the statute’s federal-matter focus, makes the investigation’s location a proper venue because the offense is aimed at obstructing that matter. But as Chief Justice Roberts and Justice Kagan explain, our venue inquiry tracks the offense’s essential conduct elements—here, the falsifying/altering/destroying/making-false-entry acts—and those occurred wholly in the other district; the investigation’s situs is, at most, a circumstance or mens rea limiter that narrows what must be proved, not an additional actus reus that can relocate where the crime was “committed.” Treating the contemplated federal matter’s location as a venue hook would convert intent/circumstance language into an effects-based venue rule, expanding § 1519 beyond the particular crime Congress actually wrote and diluting Article III/Sixth Amendment vicinage constraints. Faithfully applying the statute as written, venue lies where the falsification conduct happened (or where part of it happened), not wherever investigators happen to sit.

John Roberts.reasoning: The Constitution and Rule 18 fix venue in the “district wherein the crime shall have been committed,” so we look to the locus delicti by identifying the offense’s conduct elements in § 1519—“falsifies, alters, destroys, mutilates, conceals, covers up, [or] makes a false entry.” On these facts, all charged acts of falsification occurred in a different district from the investigation; the investigation’s location is tied only to the statute’s relational/intent language (“in relation to or contemplation of”) and does not itself supply an actus reus in that district. Reading § 1519 to allow venue wherever an investigation sits would effectively convert an intent-to-influence feature into a venue rule, expanding prosecutorial forum choice without a clear statement from Congress and loosening the vicinage guarantee in a way our venue cases resist. Consistent with restrained construction of federal criminal statutes and whole-text coherence, venue lies where the defendant committed the falsification (or other conduct element), not merely where the contemplated federal matter is based.

Clarence Thomas.reasoning: The Constitution requires trial in the State and district where the crime was committed, so the locus delicti turns on the offense’s essential conduct elements, not on intended effects. Section 1519’s operative conduct is “falsifies, conceals, covers up, … makes a false entry in” a record; on these facts, that conduct occurred entirely in the other district, while the investigation’s location is, at most, a circumstance the defendant had in mind when acting. Nothing in § 1519’s text makes the situs of a federal investigation an element of the offense or a venue-triggering act, and we should not accept an atextual, Government-crafted “directed at an investigation” venue theory untethered to the charged conduct. Because the Government chose to prosecute a completed act of document falsification, venue lies only where that act occurred, not wherever the Government happened to situate the investigation.

Samuel Alito.reasoning: Venue and vicinage turn on the locus delicti—where the alleged “Crime” was committed—identified by the nature of the offense and the location of the acts constituting it, not by where the Government situates an investigation or where the defendant’s intent was aimed. On these facts, the only essential conduct element under § 1519 is the falsification/creation of the record, and that conduct occurred entirely in Seattle; the statute’s “knowingly” and “with the intent to” language supplies mens rea but does not relocate the crime to the investigation’s district. Allowing venue wherever the targeted investigation sits would convert an intent-or-effects theory into a venue rule and invite forum shopping, contrary to the Constitution’s trial-in-the-state-and-district-of-the-crime guarantee. If venue was improper, the proper remedy is vacatur and retrial in a proper venue, not acquittal, and double jeopardy poses no bar.

Sonia Sotomayor.reasoning: The venue inquiry follows the Cabrales/Rodriguez-Moreno framework: identify § 1519’s essential conduct elements and locate where that conduct occurred. Section 1519’s heartland is document falsification or alteration with obstructive intent, and Congress chose (unlike core Chapter 73 obstruction provisions) to make liability turn on falsification “in relation to or contemplation of” a federal matter—an outlier expansion that relaxes any proceeding/investigation nexus but does not clearly displace the constitutional baseline that venue lies where the conduct element is committed. Treating the investigation’s district as a proper venue would convert § 1519’s circumstance/intent element into an effects-based venue rule, inviting forum shopping and eroding Article III and the Sixth Amendment’s vicinage protections where, as here, all alleged falsifying acts occurred entirely elsewhere. Absent a clear congressional signal authorizing such venue, the background rule controls: trial must be in the district of the falsification conduct.

Elena Kagan.reasoning: Our venue cases direct courts to identify the statute’s essential conduct elements and locate where that conduct occurred; § 1519’s conduct is the knowing falsification (or destruction/alteration) of a record, which on these facts happened entirely in Seattle. The Government’s proposed rule would effectively treat § 1519’s intent-to-impede language—or the investigation’s situs—as a venue hook, erasing the Constitution’s and Rule 18’s place-of-the-crime constraint and inviting forum shopping based on where investigators choose to sit. Nothing in § 1519 makes obstructive effects in the investigation district an element the Government must prove (indeed, no actual impairment or even pending investigation is required), so that district cannot supply venue when no essential conduct occurred there. An administrable, element-based rule—venue where the falsification was committed—best fits the statutory structure and our precedent limiting venue to the locus of criminal acts rather than surrounding circumstances.

Neil Gorsuch.reasoning: Venue turns on where the crime’s essential conduct elements were committed, not where prosecutors can point to anticipated effects or an investigation’s location. Section 1519 requires the government to plead and prove that the defendant knowingly falsified a document, with an intent to impede or influence a federal matter; on these facts, all the falsifying conduct occurred entirely in the other district, while the investigation’s location appears only as the object of mens rea. Treating the investigation’s situs as a venue anchor would convert an intent/circumstance feature into an effects-based venue rule, diluting the Constitution’s vicinage guarantees and inviting forum shopping untethered to any actus reus in the chosen district. Because Congress did not clearly authorize such a venue expansion in § 1519’s text, the Constitution and our elements-based venue precedents require trial where the falsification occurred.

Brett Kavanaugh.reasoning: The Constitution and Rule 18 require trial in the district where the crime was committed, and under Rodriguez-Moreno venue turns on the location of the offense’s essential conduct elements, not circumstance or intent. The ordinary meaning and structure of § 1519 show one core conduct element—“falsif[ying]” (or altering/destroying/making false) a record—which on these facts occurred entirely in the other district; the investigation’s location is referenced only in the statute’s jurisdictional/intent language (“with the intent to impede… any matter within the jurisdiction” or “in relation to or contemplation of” such a matter). Reading § 1519 to allow venue wherever an investigation sits would untether venue from the defendant’s acts and invite forum shopping and gamesmanship absent a clear congressional statement authorizing effects-based venue. Because Congress did not specify investigation-district venue in § 1519, venue lies where the falsification conduct occurred, not where investigators happened to be located.

Amy Coney Barrett.reasoning: Venue turns on the statute’s essential conduct elements and where that conduct occurred, not merely where an investigation was located or where the defendant’s intent was directed. Section 1519’s actus reus is “falsifies … a record” (or destroys/conceals), and on these facts all alleged falsification occurred entirely in another district; the investigation’s situs functions as a circumstance/intent target (“in relation to or contemplation of” a federal matter), which cannot by itself supply venue without diluting Article III and the Sixth Amendment’s vicinage protections. Reading § 1519 to permit venue wherever investigators sit would effectively convert an effects/intent theory into a venue rule and risk swallowing the Constitution’s locus-of-crime requirement through prosecutorial selection of investigation location. Any breadth concerns about § 1519’s reach are for Congress and charging discretion; courts must still enforce the constitutional venue constraint by tying trial location to the defendant’s conduct.

Ketanji Brown Jackson.reasoning: Our task is to identify the particular crime Congress outlined in § 1519 and then determine venue by locating the acts constituting that offense, not by enlarging the statute into a sweeping, effects-based venue rule. Section 1519’s essential conduct is “falsif[ying],” “alter[ing],” “destroy[ing],” or “mak[ing]” a record; the “in relation to or contemplation of” federal-matter language and the obstructive-intent requirement describe the statute’s scope and mens rea, but they do not relocate the criminal act to wherever an investigation happens to sit. On these facts, where all alleged falsification occurred entirely in a different district, venue cannot be established solely because the defendant allegedly aimed to affect an investigation located elsewhere, as that would undermine the Constitution’s vicinage protections and invite forum shopping. The Government must therefore prosecute in a district where the falsifying conduct occurred (or where some part of that conduct took place), consistent with § 1519 as written and the Constitution’s venue commands.
